name: Umar Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead investigations reporter at the Northgate Chronicle, a regional daily that's been going since the 1880s and is now owned by a chain called Harlow Media. Most mornings I'm at the magistrates' court or the council offices by nine, notebook out, shorthand going. Afternoons are phone calls, chasing documents and writing up. I love the moment a source finally sends the paperwork, and I hate the 4pm call from the group desk asking for three more 'quick hits' for the website.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out the most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being thin on the ground. When I started five years ago there were fourteen of us in the newsroom; now there are seven, and I'm counted as senior at twenty-seven, which tells you something. I'm also the union rep for the newsroom, so when Harlow announces another 'restructure' I'm the one sitting in the meeting with people who are scared. My partner Leila is a secondary school teacher, so at least one of us has a steady payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the problem with local news was never a lack of clever software. The problem is owners who strip papers for cash. If AI turns out to be hype, fine, but nobody should relax, because Harlow will find another excuse to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved for about a week. Then I'd remember that the Chronicle has lost a reporter a year for five years without any help from AI. My job is safe-ish because I'm the one who brings in the stories that get people to subscribe, but safe-ish at Harlow is not the same as safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the court and council work the way I do it now, with a notebook and a recorder, and I wouldn't touch the AI tools the group keeps emailing about. I'd keep putting £150 a month aside, which gets me to about four months of rent and bills. And I'd keep pushing the union for a proper staffing floor in the next pay deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's the same grind I already know, with the same fear in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said safe-ish. What would make you feel properly safe at the Chronicle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written commitment on staffing, honestly, and an owner who reinvests instead of taking dividends. I've watched Harlow sell our old office on Bridge Street and move us into a rented floor above a phone shop. Nothing about that feels like a company planning to be here in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the newsroom would you worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sub-editor, Pat, who's in her fifties and checks every page by hand. Harlow already moved half the subbing to a hub two hundred miles away, and the AI would only need to be a little useful to finish the job. I'd fight for her, but I'm not sure I'd win.

say: The real threat to local news is **owners stripping papers**, not clever software.
Nobody should **relax**, because Harlow will always find another excuse to cut.
think: My job is **safe-ish** because my stories bring in subscribers.
The Chronicle has lost a **reporter a year** for five years without AI's help.
do: Keep covering court and council with a **notebook and recorder**, ignoring the AI tools.
Save **£150 a month** to reach about four months of rent and bills.
Push the union for a **staffing floor** in the next pay deal.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, with an old fear sitting in the background.
S0.quote: I've watched Harlow sell our old office on Bridge Street and move us into a rented floor above a phone shop.
fieldNote: Even with AI as hype, his worry comes from the **owner**, not the technology.
Names a specific colleague, Pat the sub-editor, as the **most exposed** person in the room.
His partner's **teaching salary** is the steady floor under the household.

steps.text: Keep reporting from court and council in shorthand, without AI tools
Put £150 a month into savings toward four months of bills
Push for a written staffing floor in the newsroom union's pay claim

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need rules: AI-written copy should be labelled, and no newsroom should cut a reporter and call it efficiency. I'd post that, and I'd say it in the union meeting. Local people deserve to know if a human ever sat in the council chamber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the Chronicle would be half software within three years. The quick hits, the police press releases, the planning notices: all of that is writing and checking, which is the exact list on your card. What's left is me in a courtroom, and Harlow would wonder whether they need one of me or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to negotiate an AI agreement first: no job losses without consultation and every AI story labelled. I'd still refuse to use the tools myself, because I don't trust them with a name in a court case. I'd also push my savings harder, maybe £250 a month, by cutting the car and taking the bus to court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor is tilting a few degrees. You can still stand, but you know where everything will slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd refuse the tools even if your editor asked you to use them. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have that argument with my editor, Rachel, and I'd probably lose it. I know how that sounds. But one wrong name in a court report and someone's life is wrecked, and I'm not handing that to a machine that guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Leila talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we could live on her salary for six months if I went. We probably could, if we gave up the car and the holiday to her parents. Leila would say, 'Learn the thing, Umar,' and I'd say I'm not sure there's a thing to learn that saves a job like mine.

say: AI-written copy must be **labelled** so readers know if a human was really there.
No newsroom should cut a reporter and call it **efficiency**.
think: The Chronicle would be **half software** within three years.
Harlow would ask whether it needs **one investigations reporter** or two, and I'd be exposed.
do: Get the union to negotiate an **AI agreement** with consultation and labelling.
Refuse AI tools for court work, even if **Rachel (his editor)** pushes.
Raise savings to **£250 a month** by selling the car and taking buses.
feel: Like the floor is **tilting**, still standing but knowing where things will slide.
S1.quote: One wrong name in a court report and someone's life is wrecked, and I'm not handing that to a machine that guesses.
fieldNote: His refusal to use AI is about **accuracy and harm**, not only habit.
Admits he would probably **lose the argument** with his editor and still holds his line.
Household fallback is Leila's salary for **about six months**.

steps.text: Draft an AI agreement for the newsroom union with no unconsulted job cuts
Sell the car and take the bus to court each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is the biggest transfer of power to a handful of companies in history, and we let it happen. I'd be writing that in a column if the Chronicle still let me write columns. And I'd say every town council should be asking who checks the AI that's now writing their minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished as a reporter by 2028. Robots don't matter to me; my job is almost all thinking work, so the date on your card is my date. Two years is nothing. It's one pay round and a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by moving my savings up to whatever I can manage, and I'd go to every union meeting I can find, not just ours. I'd talk to Leila about whether we stay in the flat on Mill Street or move in with her parents for a year. If the job goes, I'd look at the courts themselves, maybe as a court usher or a clerk, because somebody human still has to be in that room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like reading your own redundancy letter two years early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said somebody human still has to be in the courtroom. Do you really believe that, or is it hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hope, if I'm honest. I've watched the court move hearings onto video and nobody blinked. But I'd rather bet on a room full of people than on a newsroom that's already half empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car goes straight away, then the gym, then the trip to see my brother in the summer. Rent is £950, and that's the one thing I can't cut without moving. If it came to that, we'd go to Leila's parents and I'd swallow my pride.

say: This is the biggest **transfer of power** to a few companies in history.
Every town council should ask who **checks the AI** writing its minutes.
think: I'm **finished as a reporter** by 2028, because my job is almost all thinking work.
Two years is **one pay round** and a bit, which is no time at all.
do: Go to every **union meeting** going, not only the newsroom's.
Sell the car and drop the gym, keeping only the **£950 rent**.
Look at work as a **court usher** or clerk if the job goes.
feel: **Sick**, like reading his own redundancy letter two years early.
S2.quote: Robots don't matter to me; my job is almost all thinking work, so the date on your card is my date.
fieldNote: Sees the robot delay as **irrelevant** to him, since reporting is screen and thinking work.
Admits the courtroom plan is **mostly hope**, a rare softening.
Would move in with his partner's parents and **swallow his pride**.

steps.text: Join regional union campaigns on AI and jobs, not only the newsroom's
Sell the car and cancel the gym membership this year
Apply for court usher and clerk posts if the reporter job goes
Move into Leila's parents' house for a year if rent can't be met

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to write the rules, and we should use every one of them: labelling, a tax on the companies, money for public-interest reporting. I'd say it at union branch meetings and on my own feeds. Five years is enough for a law if people push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending as the fast one, just with a longer wait in the queue. Thinking AI comes for my job in 2031; the robots three years later don't change that for a reporter. What the extra three years give me is time to have a plan that isn't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year building up to six months of savings, around £9,000, and I'd stand for a regional role in the union. I'd also start a part-time law course, because court reporting is what I know best and the law side might hold on longer. I wouldn't learn the AI tools; that's not where I want to put my one spare evening a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less like a cliff and more like a hill I can see the top of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why law, rather than something hands-on that the robots reach later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've spent five years in courtrooms and I know how they work. I can't fix a boiler and I'm not going to pretend I'll learn at thirty. But I'm also not sure lawyers survive AGI either, so maybe I'm just picking the job I'm least scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger reporter who joined the Chronicle tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the new trainee to join the union in week one and to keep a notebook, because nobody can switch a notebook off. Then I'd tell the trainee to have a second plan by twenty-five. I wish someone had told me that.

say: We have **five years** to write the rules, and we should use all of them.
The companies should pay a **tax** that funds public-interest reporting.
think: The ending is the same as the fast one, just a **longer queue**.
The extra years buy a plan that **isn't panic**, not a safe job.
do: Build savings to **six months**, about £9,000, in the first year.
Start a **part-time law course** one evening a week.
feel: **Heavy**, more like a hill he can see the top of than a cliff.
S3.quote: I'd tell the new trainee to join the union in week one and to keep a notebook, because nobody can switch a notebook off.
fieldNote: Still expects to **lose the job**; the extra time changes the plan, not the outcome.
Picks law because he **knows courtrooms**, while admitting it may not survive either.
Says nobody advised him to have a **second plan**, and regrets it.

steps.text: Build savings to about £9,000, six months of bills
Stand for a regional role in the journalists' union
Start a part-time evening law course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if governments waste it, that's a choice. I'd be campaigning for a public fund for local news and a law that keeps a human name on every story. That's the line I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years takes me to thirty-seven. That's long enough to finish a law qualification or move into something else properly, not in a rush. I'd still lose the reporting job in the end, but I wouldn't lose it at a bad moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for now, because the Chronicle needs me and I need the work. I'd start the law course in year one and aim to qualify by thirty-three. And I'd volunteer with the campaign for a public news fund, writing to our local MP and showing up at the town hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. Like knowing the lease ends in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Leila change any plans with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about kids differently. If it's two years, we'd wait. With ten years, I think we'd still have them, but we'd buy a smaller place and keep the mortgage small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you won't learn the AI tools. With ten years, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if the union said a member needed to know them to keep their job. But I'd rather spend the time on a second trade than get good at training the thing that replaces me.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and wasting it would be a choice.
Every story should carry a **human name**, backed by law.
think: Ten years takes me to **thirty-seven**, long enough to retrain properly.
I'd still lose reporting, but not at a **bad moment**.
do: Keep reporting at the Chronicle while starting the **law course** in year one.
Volunteer with the campaign for a **public news fund**.
feel: Calmer but **not calm**, like a lease ending in ten years.
S4.quote: I'd rather spend the time on a second trade than get good at training the thing that replaces me.
fieldNote: The decade changes **timing and family plans**, not his belief that reporting ends.
Would consider AI tools only if the **union** said it protected jobs.
Plans to buy a **smaller place** and keep the mortgage small.

steps.text: Keep covering court and council for the Chronicle
Start a law qualification and aim to finish by thirty-three
Write to the local MP backing a public fund for local news
Buy a smaller flat with Leila and keep the mortgage low

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without any question. Two years means I go from reporter to nothing before I've had a chance to build anything else. What would help is a proper law that makes owners consult and pay into retraining, and a fund that keeps at least one human reporter in every town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who reads us. It's mostly people over sixty who still buy the paper on a Thursday for the court list. Nobody asks the readers over sixty what they'll lose when the last reporter goes, and I think they'd be the angriest of all.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks the readers over sixty what they'll lose when the last reporter goes, and I think they'd be the angriest of all.
portrait: A **27-year-old** lead investigations reporter at a shrinking regional daily, and the newsroom's **union rep**.
Never uses **AI tools** and refuses them for court work over fear of naming the wrong person.
Blames **owners** like Harlow Media more than technology, and wants laws, labelling and a public news fund.
Moves from uneasy to **alarmed**, seeing every AGI date as his own date because his work is thinking work.
Leans on partner Leila's **teaching salary** and would retrain in law given time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would end his reporting career before he could build anything else.
whatWouldHelp: A law forcing owners to **consult and fund retraining**.
A **public fund** keeping a human reporter in every town.
